requirements.text: The contractor must develop the curriculum for and administer the AI Prep program for Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) and/or Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs).

ambiguities.description: The text does not define eligibility thresholds for "low-income" or "barriers to employment", nor who verifies them; a bidder would ask what income limits and eligibility documentation OSWD requires, since this drives recruitment and enrollment design.

It is unclear whether a bidder may propose for both Track A and Track B, and whether the two contracts are awarded to two different administrators or one administrator could hold both; this affects staffing and pricing strategy.

The text does not define who pays the participant stipends and internship wages (the administrator's budget versus the host employers), nor the stipend amount or duration, which materially changes the bid price.
The scale of the program is unspecified: no target number of students served, cohort size, internship count, or program duration is given, so the bidder cannot size staffing and cost.

The text does not say how the up-to-$2M per track award is to be split between training delivery and participant stipends, nor what stipend amount or duration is expected, which drives the price build-up. The bidder would ask what portion of the award must go to stipends and at what per-participant rate.

The number of participants to be trained and supported within the $2M per track cap is not stated, so unit costs and staffing cannot be sized. The bidder would ask for a target enrollment/participant count per track.

The renewal or extension terms are open: the text does not state the maximum total duration or the criteria/thresholds for performance-based renewal. The bidder would ask how long an extension may run and what performance measures trigger it.

The text does not define "low-income" (e.g., a specific income threshold or eligibility standard such as federal poverty level or area median income), which determines participant recruitment targets and reporting; the bidder would ask which definition or standard applies.

The text does not define what counts as a "graduate" (completion criteria, attendance thresholds) or the measurement window for securing internships or employment, which affects program design and outcome tracking; the bidder would ask how graduation and placement are defined and measured.
"Strong track record for workforce development in AI or similar fields" is undefined and gates eligibility; the bidder would ask what evidence or minimum experience qualifies.

The RFP does not say how experience in a domain is demonstrated or measured (e.g., years of experience, number of students served, contract values), so a bidder cannot tell whether its track record qualifies or what evidence to submit.

The text refers to "one track" and "both tracks" without defining what the tracks are or how many exist, which determines whether the $2M or $4M cap applies; the bidder would ask how many tracks there are and what each covers.

ESD may deny reimbursement of expenses "deemed ineligible" but the text does not define eligibility criteria or whether reimbursement is the only payment mechanism; the bidder would ask what expense categories are eligible and how payment is structured.

The text does not state the program duration that the budget must be mapped to, nor the total funding cap, so a bidder cannot size the budget or the stipend level; the bidder would ask what the program period and maximum award amount are.

The required participant stipend level is not quantified or bounded (per-participant amount, number of participants, or cap), which directly drives cost; the bidder would ask what stipend level is expected or permitted.

The text says there is no cost-match requirement yet states applicants receive additional points for cost-matching, without specifying how much match earns how many points; a bidder would ask how the scoring credit for cost match is calculated.

The chunk refers to "Proposed definition" without stating what definition is being defined or where the alternative definition must be submitted; a bidder would ask which definition this refers to and in what form the alternative and its justification must be provided.

The exact list of data points is left to ESD and will only be fixed during contract negotiation, so the bidder cannot know the full reporting scope or effort to price; the bidder would ask what the final data-point list and reporting frequency/format will be.

The text does not define how 'low-income' is determined (e.g., income threshold or program eligibility criterion), which affects how participants are tracked and reported; the bidder would ask for the definition to apply.

The Corporation reserves the right to change any of the dates, so the bidder cannot rely on the stated schedule; the bidder would ask whether the submission deadline and contract start date are firm or subject to change and how changes will be communicated.
The anticipated debriefing timeframe is listed as TBD, leaving the post-award schedule open; the bidder would ask when debriefings will occur.

The cover letter must state an "annual budget" and "annual number of participants served" without specifying which fiscal year, currency, or whether the figures cover the whole organization or only AI-related programs; a bidder would ask which period and scope to report.

"Substantive, skill-based, college-level or accelerated immersive training" is not defined, so it is unclear what evidence (hours, credentials, accreditation, completion rates) will be accepted as demonstrating it; a bidder would ask what proof of training depth is expected.

The experience items are requested only "if applicable" or "if not already addressed", so it is unclear whether a Respondent with no college-student or New York-market experience must state that explicitly or may omit the item, and whether omission costs points under the 25-point Experience criterion.
The text does not define what counts as "low-income" (e.g., income threshold or program eligibility standard) or what "additional supports" covers, so Respondents cannot tell what evidence to report.

The text requires a monthly timeline running "through the completion of internships or full-time jobs by the first cohort" but gives no program start date, cohort launch date or overall contract period, so the bidder cannot anchor the monthly schedule; the bidder would ask for the intended program start date and the required end date for the first cohort's placements.

The proposal must state a proposed stipend level and cohort size, but the text gives no funding envelope, per-participant budget or cap, so the bidder cannot judge what stipend and cohort size are affordable; the bidder would ask whether there is a maximum award or per-participant cost limit.

The metrics are listed without definitions or a required reporting period or format: it is unclear whether "low-income" has a defined threshold, how "placement rate" is calculated (e.g., timeframe after graduation, part-time vs. full-time), and what annual period the estimates cover. A bidder would ask the issuer to define each metric and the reporting basis.

The bracketed note instructs the "originator" to establish a uniform schedule for complex cost structures, but it is unclear whether Respondents must follow a prescribed fee schedule format and who the originator is; a bidder would ask whether a mandatory cost template exists and where it is provided.

The Technical Proposal must include a "Cost of Services" section, yet cost is normally submitted separately from technical content; the bidder would ask whether pricing belongs in the Technical Proposal or in a separate cost proposal, and whether a cost section here would breach the "no information beyond what is specifically requested" limit.

The "Diversity Practices Questionnaire" is listed as a required Technical Proposal component but no form or content is provided in this text; the bidder would ask where the questionnaire is obtained and what responses it requires.

The text says failure to submit any listed item may result in rejection, but the items are introduced with "should" rather than "must"; a bidder would ask whether each item is strictly mandatory or whether some are conditional (e.g., the ST-220-CA form versus the affidavit alternative).

client_situation.text: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD), a New York State economic development corporation whose mission is to promote a growing state economy, encourage business investment and job creation, and support diverse local economies through loans, grants, tax credits, real estate development and marketing.

ESD's Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD) was created under Governor Hochul's April 2022 $350 million workforce development investment and is charged with aligning workforce efforts to employer needs and creating economic opportunity for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented workers.

ESD identifies Artificial Intelligence as one of the state's highest-growth sectors, citing Cornell Tech research, companies using AI for analytics, automation and decision-making, and the state-backed Empire AI initiative.

ESD's stated pain point is that rapid AI advancement risks widening economic inequality because many well-paying AI jobs require specialized education and technical training that lower-income New Yorkers cannot access.
ESD also points to tech recruiting practices that favor students at elite schools and those with personal connections to prominent technology companies as a barrier AI Prep is meant to level.

ESD currently has no AI Prep program in place: OSWD is launching AI Prep as a new applied training program and seeks to award contracts to up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum and administer it.

The procurement is subject to a restricted period under the Procurement Lobbying Law running until contract approval, during which respondents may contact only the designated contacts Julia Borukhov and Jordan Kaplan at AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov.

goal.text: ESD wants up to two program administrators to design the curriculum for and deliver AI Prep across two tracks: Track A "AI Prep 4 Internships" for low-income matriculating undergraduates and Track B "AI Prep 4 Jobs" for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment.
Track A requires a comprehensive AI technology training program for low-income college students that includes paid internship placements and builds a talent pipeline for AI employers.

Track B requires an industry-informed AI training program, delivered as an accelerated course or bootcamp as an alternative to traditional degree programs, that connects low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment to full-time AI jobs.

Deliverables common to both tracks include targeted outreach and recruitment, an application and assessment process, online AI courses built with industry and researcher input, participant stipends and wrap-around supports such as mentors or success coaches, and employer relationship building to generate placements.

The contract runs for an initial term of up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need and availability of funds, and the anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026.
ESD will invest up to $2M per track, up to $4M total, to train and provide stipends for participants.

Awarded administrators must track and report data including applicant, enrollment and completion counts with low-income percentages, paid internship and full-time placement rates, participating colleges and employer partners, with the exact list set during contract negotiation.

success_criteria.text: Proposals are scored out of a maximum of 100 points by an ESD selection committee, allocated as Firm Qualifications 15, Experience 25, Project Plan 30, Cost of Services 20 and Diversity Practices 10.
The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for applicants proposing to serve more than 400, and over 50% of participants must be low-income.
The majority of program graduates must secure paid internships or full-time employment in artificial intelligence or a closely related field.

The Project Plan must estimate annual performance on three metrics — total participants served, percentage of low-income participants completing the curriculum, and paid internship or full-time job placement rate — justified by historical experience or partner commitments.

Questions must be submitted by email to AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov by August 29, 2025, with ESD responses due September 12, 2025, and proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, with late proposals rejected.
Interviews, if necessary, are scheduled for the first week of November 2025 and the successful respondent is to be announced on November 14, 2025.

Applicants must have experience in at least three of four domains to qualify: academic services to college students, administering high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.
Cost matching is not required but earns additional points in scoring, and the extent of any match must be shown in the budget template.

constraints.text: Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period will not be considered, and indirect costs are not an allowable expense.

The budget must be mapped to the program duration and cover Staff Salary and Benefits, Wraparound Supports and the proposed participant stipend level, and other costs such as curriculum development, marketing and events.

Proposals must be uploaded as a two-part submission (separate Administrative and Technical Proposal subfolders in a main folder named "company name – RFP title – date of Submission") to the Dropbox at https://www.dropbox.com/request/AIPrep; fax, hardcopy and email submissions are not accepted.

The Administrative Proposal must include, in order, the Non-Collusive Bidding Certification, Conflict of Interest Attestation, State Finance Law §§139-j/139-k forms, Vendor Responsibility Questionnaire, Iran Divestment Act Statement, EO-16 and EO-177 certifications, OCSD-1/OCSD-2/OCSD-4 diversity forms, the Encouraging Use of NYS Businesses form, ST-220-CA or affidavit, and a W-9, and missing any may cause rejection.

The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, requiring an MWBE Utilization Plan and an SDVOB Utilization Plan (Form OCSD-4) with the proposal and quarterly and monthly compliance reporting thereafter.

The selected respondent must carry Commercial General Liability of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate, Commercial Auto of $1M if a vehicle is used, Sexual Abuse and Molestation insurance of $1M, and statutory Workers' Compensation, Employer's Liability and Disability coverage, naming ESD as additional insured with a waiver of subrogation.

Appendix A "ESD IT Security Standard Brief" and Appendix B "Diversity Practices Questionnaire" are referenced by the RFP but their contents are not included in the RFP text, so bidders must obtain them separately.

Contractor staff are subject to ESD approval, staff continuity is expected through project completion, and any subcontracting not identified in the proposal requires prior written approval of the State Project Manager.

solution.summary: Empire State Development (ESD) receives a single, integrated AI Prep program built and delivered by a lead administrator that designs the curriculum, recruits and supports participants, and places them into paid internships (Track A) and full-time AI jobs (Track B). The solution is a build-and-operate engagement: curriculum and assessment assets are developed in a mobilisation phase, then cohorts are recruited, trained online, coached and placed across the 18-month initial term beginning January 1, 2026, with a data and reporting spine running throughout. Delivery is organised in four phases — mobilise and finalise design, recruit and launch the first cohort, deliver and place at scale, and sustain and report — each with monthly milestones and performance estimates against ESD's three metrics. The team is a lead administrator with a program director, curriculum and instructional design staff, employer partnership leads, success coaches and a compliance/reporting function, supported by named subcontractors for outreach and employer engagement. Pricing is built bottom-up within the $2M per track / $4M total cap, with stipends and wraparound supports as explicit budget lines and no indirect costs. Governance, MWBE/SDVOB participation, insurance and contract compliance are handled by a dedicated compliance workstream that runs from proposal submission through quarterly and monthly reporting.

components.title: Program design, curriculum and assessment build
components.description: We design an industry-informed AI curriculum built with employer and researcher input, delivered as online courses with defined technical skills and learning milestones (R014, R025). The build covers the full AI technology training program for low-income college students including the internship component (R009), the accelerated bootcamp alternative to a degree for Track B (R007), and the immersive schedule that can run part-time or full-time (R027). We define the credentials awarded on completion (R031) and embed skill-attainment evaluation metrics at each milestone (R029). The curriculum is developed in the mobilisation phase and refreshed each cohort against employer feedback, and the whole delivery plan is scoped to the 18-month initial term with any renewal or extension treated as a separately priced option (R035).

components.description: We run a targeted outreach and recruitment strategy for low-income students and for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented New Yorkers (R011, R024), reaching New Yorkers underrepresented in tech who cannot reasonably access training on their own (R008). A structured application and evaluation process screens and selects participants (R012), and a needs assessment at intake identifies and addresses each participant's barriers to success (R013). Track A recruitment targets low-income matriculating undergraduates (R006); Track B recruitment targets low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment (R007).

components.title: Training delivery, coaching and participant supports
components.description: We deliver and manage the AI training program cohort by cohort (R015), with professional development support for trainees throughout training (R030). Every participant receives a stipend and wraparound supports including mentors and career coaches with industry expertise (R016), and the budget carries the proposed stipend level and wraparound supports as explicit lines (R051). Track A students are trained specifically to secure paid internships at leading tech companies (R006, R021), and Track B participants are connected to full-time AI jobs through the accelerated pathway (R007, R032).

components.title: Employer partnerships and placement engine
components.description: We cultivate and maintain relationships with leading industry employers to inform training content and generate paid internship opportunities (R018), and we help students secure paid internships (R017). Internships are structured so students hone newly acquired AI skills through real-world experience and networking that leads to full-time roles (R022), and we provide full-time job connection support in AI-related fields (R032). The program creates direct education-to-industry pathways and builds a talent pipeline for AI employers (R010), with placement support tailored to New York State technology companies (R021).

We estimate annual performance on total participants served, low-income completion percentage and placement rate, justified by historical results and partner commitments (R090), and we report against the 250-participant minimum, the over-50% low-income target and the majority-placement target (R038, R040, R041).

components.title: Procurement communications and post-award administration
components.description: We manage every procurement communication through the designated channel: all questions about the RFP are submitted by email to AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov by the August 29, 2025 deadline (R060), and we accept that questions submitted after the deadline given in the Schedule of Dates may not be answered (R128). We review ESD's posted responses of September 12, 2025 before finalising the proposal. After award, if we are unsuccessful we request a debriefing within 15 calendar days of ESD's notification that our proposal was not selected (R259), and if we are successful we hold the contract on the 18-month initial term with renewal or extension at ESD's discretion based on performance, need and availability of funds (R035).

claims.text: Questions are due by email to AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov by August 29, 2025, with ESD responses due September 12, 2025, proposals due 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, and the successful respondent announced November 14, 2025.

assumptions.text: The bid is submitted for both tracks under one lead administrator, with a single program management office and shared services, priced at no more than $2M per track and $4M in total.

Low-income eligibility is defined as Pell-grant eligibility for Track A and household income at or below 200% of the federal poverty level for Track B, verified by documentation at application, subject to ESD's confirmation at contract negotiation.

Participant stipends are paid from the administrator's award budget, while internship wages are paid by host employers, and the stipend is set at a per-participant rate that leaves the majority of the $2M per track for training delivery and supports.

The program is sized at approximately 400 participants per track over the 18-month term, in cohorts of 50 running on a rolling part-time and full-time schedule, which is the basis for staffing and unit costs.
The budget is mapped to the 18-month initial term from January 1, 2026, and any renewal or extension is priced separately at the same unit rates rather than assumed in the base price.

A graduate is a participant who completes all curriculum milestones and the final assessment, and placement is measured as paid internship or full-time AI-related employment secured within six months of completion.

The final reporting data set and reporting frequency will be fixed at contract negotiation, and the solution is built on a configurable data model so added fields and cadences do not require re-platforming.

The Appendix A ESD IT Security Standard Brief and Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire will be obtained from ESD and applied as issued, with the platform configured to meet Appendix A controls and the questionnaire completed from our existing diversity practices record.
The cost-match credit is pursued through a modest documented cash and in-kind match shown in the budget template, on the basis that the RFP gives no scoring formula for match.

The 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB goals are treated as applying to total contract value and as requiring demonstrated good faith efforts rather than guaranteed attainment, with waiver requests filed on Form OCSD-5 only after consulting the Designated Contacts.

OSC review under Public Authorities Law §2879-a is assumed to apply given the award size, so mobilisation is planned to begin on award with curriculum build completing before the January 1, 2026 start and no reliance on pre-approval spend.

All subcontractors, including outreach partners and employer engagement specialists, are named in the proposal with scope and estimated value so the proposal-identified subcontracting exception applies without further written approval.

The Technical Proposal carries a Cost of Services section limited to the line-by-line price schedule requested, resolving the tension with the instruction not to include information beyond what is requested.
Schedule A concerns are submitted in writing with the Administrative Proposal and Schedule A documentation itself is kept out of the proposal, so both instructions are satisfied.

The construction-scoped equal employment opportunity programme obligation is treated as not attaching to this AI training and placement scope, with our non-discrimination and EEO policy flowed down to all subcontractors instead.

risks.title: Program scale and stipend level undefined against a hard $2M per track cap
risks.description: The RFP caps funding at $2M per track but never states a target participant count, cohort size, stipend amount or stipend duration, while also requiring a 250-participant minimum, priority above 400, and a majority-placement outcome. The proposed solution assumes roughly 400 participants per track in cohorts of 50 with a stipend rate that leaves most of the award for delivery — an assumption, not a settled fact. If ESD expects a higher stipend or a larger cohort, the unit economics break and the bid is either unaffordable or under-scoped.
risks.justification: The cap is firm and disqualifying (budgets above $2M per track are not considered) while the participant count and stipend level that drive cost are absent from the RFP; the solution's 400-per-track sizing is explicitly an inference.
risks.mitigation: Submit a written question before the August 29, 2025 deadline asking for the expected participant count per track and the expected stipend level and duration; state in the proposal the participant count, cohort size and stipend rate the price is built on, and price a lower-stipend/higher-volume variant as an option.

risks.title: Schedule A, Appendix A, Appendix B and Schedule B are not in the RFP
risks.description: Four referenced documents — Schedule A (standard contract terms), Appendix A (ESD IT Security Standard Brief), Appendix B (Diversity Practices Questionnaire) and Schedule B (MWBE requirements and procedures) — are cited but not included in the RFP text. Schedule A must be accepted as part of the executed contract, Appendix A sets the security controls the platform must meet, and Appendix B is a scored 10-point submission item. Bidding without them means pricing and designing against unknown obligations, and a missing Appendix B response risks losing points or rejection.
risks.justification: The documents are named in the RFP but absent from it, and two of them (Appendix B, Schedule A) are mandatory submission or contract-acceptance items; the solution simply assumes they will be obtained and applied as issued.
risks.mitigation: Request all four documents from AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov before the question deadline; if Appendix A or B is not released, state in the proposal the security baseline assumed and that the Diversity Practices response will be completed on the issued form, and reserve the right to adjust price once Schedule A is seen.

risks.title: Placement and completion targets depend on employer partners the bidder does not control
risks.description: The RFP requires that the majority of graduates secure paid internships or full-time AI employment, and the solution commits to that outcome while relying on host employers to create internships and pay internship wages. Employer letters of commitment are required with the proposal, but the RFP does not guarantee employer demand, and the solution's placement estimate rests on partner commitments that are not yet evidenced. A shortfall against the placement metric puts performance-based renewal and the 18-month term at risk.
risks.justification: Placement is the headline outcome metric and drives renewal, but it is delivered by third-party employers; the solution treats internship wages as employer-paid, which is an assumption the RFP does not settle.
risks.mitigation: Secure signed employer commitment letters covering a defined number of internship slots per cohort before submission, and state in the proposal a placement contingency (employer-of-record or stipend-funded internship fallback) with the cost carried in the budget.

risks.title: MWBE 30% and SDVOB 6% goals carry liquidated damages and material-breach exposure
risks.description: The contract sets a 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB participation goal, with liquidated damages equal to the shortfall for willful MWBE non-compliance and material breach for failing to use SDVOBs as planned. The solution treats the goals as requiring good faith efforts rather than guaranteed attainment, but the RFP does not settle whether the goals apply to total contract value or subcontracting spend, and the bidder's supply chain for an AI training program may have limited certified MWBE and SDVOB capacity. A shortfall exposes the bidder to withheld payment and damages.
risks.justification: The remedies are contractual and quantified (shortfall-based liquidated damages, material breach), while the base to which the goals apply and the availability of certified firms in this sector are not settled by the RFP.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD to confirm the base for the 30% and 6% goals and whether good faith efforts suffice; identify and name certified MWBE and SDVOB subcontractors in the Utilization Plans before submission, and document solicitations and non-selection reasons from day one.

risks.title: Low-income eligibility and 'graduate'/'placement' definitions are unsettled
risks.description: The RFP does not define 'low-income', 'barriers to employment', what counts as a graduate, or the window in which a placement counts, yet over 50% of participants must be low-income and the majority-placement metric drives renewal. The solution assumes Pell eligibility for Track A and 200% of the federal poverty level for Track B, and a six-month placement window — all inferences. If ESD applies a different standard at negotiation, recruitment targets, verification effort and reported outcomes all shift.
risks.justification: Multiple definitions that directly drive recruitment, verification cost and the reported metrics are left open, and the solution's definitions are explicitly marked as inferences subject to ESD confirmation.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD to confirm the income standard and documentation for each track and the definition of graduate and placement window; state the assumed definitions in the proposal and build the data model so the eligibility rule and placement window are configurable.

risks.title: OSC approval may delay contract execution past the January 1, 2026 start
risks.description: The contract is unenforceable until the Office of the State Comptroller grants any required review and approval under Public Authorities Law §2879-a, and the RFP only says such review 'may be required'. The solution plans mobilisation to begin on award with curriculum build completing before January 1, 2026 and no pre-approval spend. If OSC review runs long, the mobilisation window compresses and the first cohort launch, and therefore the 18-month delivery plan, slips.
risks.justification: Award is announced November 14, 2025 against a January 1, 2026 start, leaving roughly six weeks for OSC review and mobilisation; the RFP does not confirm whether review applies or how long it takes.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD whether OSC review is expected for this award and what start date applies if approval is delayed; state in the proposal that the curriculum build is compressed into a fixed mobilisation window and that the delivery schedule rebases from contract execution, not from the award announcement.

risks.title: Reporting scope is fixed only at contract negotiation
risks.description: The RFP leaves the final data-point list and reporting frequency to contract negotiation, while the solution commits to a configurable data spine and to quarterly and monthly compliance reporting. If ESD adds fields, cadences or formats beyond what is priced, the reporting effort grows after the price is fixed, and the solution's assumption that added fields need no re-platforming is untested.
risks.justification: The RFP states the exact list will be set during contract negotiation, so the reporting effort is unknown at bid time; the solution's configurable-model assumption is an inference, not a confirmed requirement.
risks.mitigation: State in the proposal the reporting scope and cadence the price covers, with a defined change mechanism and unit rates for added fields or reports; ask ESD at the question stage for the expected reporting frequency and format.

risks.title: Technical Proposal content limits conflict with the required Cost of Services section
risks.description: One requirement forbids including any information beyond what is specifically requested in the Technical Proposal, while another asks for a complete and clear response and the Technical Proposal must contain a Cost of Services section. The solution resolves this by limiting the Cost of Services section to the line-by-line price schedule. If ESD reads the limit strictly, narrative pricing justification could be treated as non-conforming; if read loosely, the bid may be marked incomplete.
risks.justification: The two instructions pull in opposite directions and the RFP does not say where pricing belongs; the solution's resolution is an inference rather than a stated RFP rule.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD whether pricing belongs in the Technical Proposal or a separate cost file and whether a cost narrative is permitted; keep the Cost of Services section to the requested line items and place any justification in the budget template.

risks.title: Schedule A concerns must be filed without putting Schedule A content in the proposal
risks.description: The RFP tells respondents not to include Schedule A information or documentation in the proposal, yet also requires them to review Schedule A and submit any concerns in writing with the Administrative Proposal. The solution handles this by filing concerns separately and keeping Schedule A documentation out. If ESD treats the written concerns as prohibited content, the Administrative Proposal could be found non-conforming.
risks.justification: The two instructions are in direct tension and the RFP sets no deadline or format for the written concerns, so the bidder cannot be sure the filing satisfies both.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD to confirm the format and placement of Schedule A concerns and the deadline for filing them; submit concerns as a clearly labelled separate document in the Administrative Proposal folder and state in the cover letter that no Schedule A documentation is included.

risks.title: Two-track delivery with a single team and shared services
risks.description: The solution bids both tracks under one lead administrator with a single program management office and shared services, and the RFP requires a detailed description of organisational capacity to run two programs simultaneously. Running two tracks with distinct eligibility, curriculum and placement models from one team risks overloading the program director and coaches, and the RFP does not confirm that one administrator may hold both tracks.
risks.justification: The RFP does not settle whether one administrator can hold both tracks, and the solution's single-PMO design concentrates delivery risk on a small leadership team.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD whether one administrator may be awarded both tracks; in the proposal, name separate track leads under the program director and show the capacity plan and staffing ratios per track.

risks.title: Staff approval and continuity obligations constrain a delivery team built on named specialists
risks.description: Contractor staff are subject to ESD approval, staff continuity through completion is expected, and any substitute must be presented with an experience summary and interviewed before approval. The solution commits to continuity and to naming staff in the price proposal. If a key curriculum or employer-partnership lead leaves, the replacement cycle could stall delivery and the priced staffing plan becomes inaccurate.
risks.justification: The approval and interview steps add delay to any replacement, and the solution's price is built on named roles with defined percentages of time.
risks.mitigation: Name a deputy for each key role in the proposal and state that substitutes will be pre-identified with experience summaries ready; ask ESD how quickly approval decisions will be made.

risks.title: Insurance and compliance obligations may exceed a training provider's current cover
risks.description: The selected respondent must carry $1M/$2M commercial general liability, $1M sexual abuse and molestation cover, commercial auto where a vehicle is used, and statutory workers' compensation, employer's liability and disability cover, with ESD as additional insured and a waiver of subrogation. The RFP qualifies the list as applying 'at a minimum and to the extent applicable' without saying which coverages attach to an AI training engagement. Sexual abuse and molestation cover in particular may not be in a training provider's existing programme and takes time to bind.
risks.justification: The coverages are mandatory contract conditions but the RFP does not confirm which apply to this scope, and the solution simply asserts it carries all of them.
risks.mitigation: Ask ESD which coverages are mandatory for this scope and whether the waiver of subrogation is required on all policies; obtain broker quotes for sexual abuse and molestation cover before submission and carry the premium in the budget.
